description: Derive a hypergraph whose hyperedges encode sufficient support patterns for anti-diagonal forcing, then deliberately search for long-running spanning processes. The hypothesis is that sparse but deep infection chains may recycle the same few edges many times and therefore beat denser, faster constructions on score.
mathematical_formalization: Let H_F have vertex set V(G) and hyperedges S -> e whenever there exists a local linear derivation that forces e from support contained in S union {e}. For a seed set A, let tau_H(A) be the number of rounds until closure; optimize score(G,R,T) while preferring larger tau_H(A) under the constraint cl_H(A) = V.
analogical_connections: A slow avalanche in bootstrap percolation rather than an immediate cascade.
Long proof chains that reuse a small axiom base many times.
Pipeline latency used as a proxy for structural reuse.
implementation_hypothesis: Extract approximate dependency hyperedges from the exact solver, estimate infection times quickly, and bias the outer search toward sparse constructions with unusually long closure time.
experiment_seed: On fixed small X, enumerate candidate graphs and compare score against derived hypergraph infection time to test whether longer-running instances systematically have better edge-to-coverage ratios.

closest_prior_art.title: On the Running Time of Hypergraph Bootstrap Percolation
The maximal running time of hypergraph bootstrap percolation

novelty_claim: The novelty is to treat infection time as a positive design feature for arithmetic Kakeya witnesses rather than as a complexity nuisance.
differentiation: The hypergraph papers study generic closure systems. Here the hyperedges come from exact integer-linear forcing semantics and are only a derived abstraction to guide witness search.
